statement: The Bernoulli distribution is the discrete probability distribution of a random variable $X$ that takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and the value $0$ with probability $q = 1 - p$, having probability mass function $f(k; p) = p^k (1 - p)^{1 - k}$ for $k \in \{0, 1\}$ (equivalently $f(k; p) = pk + (1 - p)(1 - k)$).

symbols.meaning: probability of outcome 0, equal to 1 - p (failure probability)

properties.why: expectation over binary outcomes gives $\Pr(X=1) \cdot 1 + \Pr(X=0) \cdot 0 = p \cdot 1 + q \cdot 0 = p$

properties.property: The variance is $\operatorname{Var}[X] = pq = p(1 - p)$
properties.why: evaluated from $\operatorname{E}[X^2] - (\operatorname{E}[X])^2 = p - p^2 = p(1 - p)$

properties.property: All raw moments are identical: $\operatorname{E}[X^k] = p$ for integer $k \ge 1$

properties.why: computed from the standardized third central moment $\operatorname{E}[((X - \operatorname{E}[X])/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}[X]})^3]$

properties.property: The entropy is $H(X) = -(q \ln q + p \ln p)$
The Fisher information with respect to $p$ is $I(p) = \frac{1}{pq} = \frac{1}{p(1 - p)}$
properties.why: the negative expected value of the second derivative of the log-likelihood function

properties.property: The sum of $n$ i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables follows a binomial distribution $\sum_{k=1}^n X_k \sim \operatorname{B}(n, p)$
properties.why: the Bernoulli distribution corresponds to the special case of a binomial trial with $n = 1$

assumptions.assumption: The random variable $X$ has binary support restricted to outcomes $\{0, 1\}$
assumptions.breaks_when: The outcomes are arbitrary non-binary values or take values other than 0 and 1

assumptions.assumption: The success parameter $p$ lies in the valid probability interval $0 \le p \le 1$
Only a single trial is performed ($n = 1$)
assumptions.breaks_when: Multiple independent trials are performed, which generalizes to a binomial distribution with $n > 1$

failure_modes.signature: Variance becomes 0, while skewness and Fisher information $I(p) = 1/(pq)$ are undefined due to division by zero
failure_modes.cause: When $p = 0$ or $p = 1$, the distribution becomes deterministic with zero variance and $pq = 0$
Occurs when $p$ approaches either 0 or 1, making one outcome vanishingly rare relative to the other
